3.0.big: Living things are built from four kinds of large molecules: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids.
points: These biological macromolecules are built from small pieces and do nearly everything in a cell: store energy, build structures, speed up reactions, and carry genetic information.

3.1.big: Small building blocks (monomers) link into chains (polymers) by removing water, and break apart by adding water back.
points: Dehydration synthesis: an –OH from one monomer and an –H from another leave as water, and the monomers bond. This builds polymers.
Hydrolysis: water is split and added back across the bond, breaking the polymer into monomers. Digestion is hydrolysis, and it releases energy.
Enzymes speed up both reactions.
3.1.tip: Dehydration = remove water to build. Hydro-lysis = water-splitting to break.

3.2.big: Carbohydrates are sugars and their polymers. They're used for quick energy, energy storage and structure.
points: Monosaccharides (simple sugars): glucose, fructose, galactose. They often form rings in water.
Disaccharides: two sugars joined by a glycosidic bond. Sucrose = glucose + fructose. Lactose = glucose + galactose. Maltose = glucose + glucose.

Polysaccharides: starch (plant energy storage: amylose and amylopectin, α-linkages), glycogen (animal storage in liver and muscle, very branched), cellulose (plant cell walls, β-1,4 linkages humans can't digest, so it's fiber), chitin (insect exoskeletons and fungal walls; contains nitrogen).

3.3.big: Lipids are hydrophobic (they don't mix with water). They store energy, form membranes, and act as hormones.
points: Triacylglycerol (triglyceride) = glycerol + 3 fatty acids: the main energy storage form in animals.

Saturated fatty acid: all single bonds, packed with hydrogen, straight, solid at room temperature (butter). Unsaturated fatty acid: one or more double bonds, kinked, liquid (oils). Omega fats (omega-3) are healthy unsaturated fats we must eat.
Trans fat: made by hydrogenating oil; the hydrogens around the double bond sit on opposite sides. Raises LDL ("bad" cholesterol).
Waxes: waterproof coatings on leaves and feathers.
Phospholipids: glycerol + 2 fatty-acid tails (hydrophobic) + a phosphate head (hydrophilic). They form the cell membrane bilayer, heads out and tails in.
Steroids: four fused rings. Cholesterol makes steroid hormones (testosterone, estradiol) and bile salts, and keeps membranes flexible.

3.4.big: Proteins do most of the work in a cell, and their job depends on their 3-D shape, which depends on their amino acid sequence.
points: Jobs: enzymes (speed up reactions), structure, transport, hormones (signals), defense (antibodies), movement.
20 amino acids, each with an amino group, a carboxyl group, and a unique R group (nonpolar, polar, or charged). They're joined by peptide bonds (carboxyl to amino) into a polypeptide.

Primary structure: the amino acid sequence. Secondary structure: the α-helix and β-pleated sheet (held by hydrogen bonds). Tertiary structure: the overall 3-D fold (R-group interactions, disulfide bonds), which usually sets the function. Quaternary structure: several polypeptides together (hemoglobin).
One changed amino acid can change everything: sickle cell anemia comes from a single swap in hemoglobin.
Denaturation: heat, pH changes or chemicals unfold a protein, so it stops working. Chaperones help proteins fold correctly.
In water-soluble proteins, polar and charged amino acids sit on the outside and nonpolar ones are tucked inside.

3.5.big: Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) store and use genetic information.
points: Building block: the nucleotide = a 5-carbon sugar + a phosphate + a nitrogen base. Nucleotides link by phosphodiester linkages into a polynucleotide.
Bases: purines (two rings: A, G) and pyrimidines (one ring: C, T, U).
Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): deoxyribose sugar, bases A T G C, a double helix with A–T and G–C pairing. Stores hereditary info, mostly in the nucleus.

Ribonucleic acid (RNA): ribose sugar, U instead of T, usually single-stranded. Messenger RNA (mRNA) carries the gene's message, ribosomal RNA (rRNA) builds ribosomes, transfer RNA (tRNA) brings amino acids, and microRNA (the smallest) regulates genes.
Transcription = DNA → mRNA. Translation = mRNA → protein.

2.why: Water leaves, taking a hydroxyl (–OH) from one nucleotide (and H from the other).

10.why: Lactose = glucose + galactose, linked by a glycosidic bond.

15.why: Estradiol and testosterone are steroid hormones made from cholesterol.

16.why: Not true: fats are hydrophobic and don't dissolve in water.

17.why: Double bonds replace hydrogens, so unsaturated fats have the fewest.

21.why: Cholesterol is used to make bile salts.

23.why: Red blood cells squeeze through tiny capillaries, and cholesterol helps keep their membranes stable yet flexible.

26.why: Polar and charged (hydrophilic) amino acids, like serine, lysine and glutamate, because they interact well with water.

28.why: A peptide bond joins one amino acid's carboxyl to the next one's amino group.

30.why: The 3-D tertiary fold usually decides what a protein does.

31.why: pH, heat and chemicals can all denature proteins.

34.why: DNA = deoxyribose, thymine (or A, G, C), and phosphate.

39.why: Water splits into H and OH, which are added to the monomers as the polymer breaks.

40.why: In dehydration synthesis, electrons end up with the OH and H that leave as water. In hydrolysis they're taken back from them as the bond reforms.

42.why: We lack the enzyme to break β-1,4 bonds.

44.why: Sucrose = glucose + fructose. Lactose = glucose + galactose. Maltose = 2 glucose.

47.why: Partial hydrogenation of oil makes trans fats, which raise LDL.

48.why: Heads face water and tails face inward: a bilayer.

51.why: Different amino acids form different bonds, giving different shapes and jobs.

52.why: The sequence folds into helices and sheets, which fold further into the 3-D tertiary shape.

53.why: Red is at about 70 kDa, higher up than green (about 10 kDa), so red is heavier.

55.why: DNA: deoxyribose and thymine. RNA: ribose and uracil.

57.why: mRNA = DNA transcript, rRNA = ribosomes, tRNA = brings amino acids, miRNA = regulates mRNA.

58.why: They assumed what gases made up the early atmosphere.

59.why: Simple gases with hydrogen and nitrogen formed amino acids.

60.why: Inorganic molecules formed amino acids and other organic molecules.

61.why: Condensing and evaporating water modeled the water cycle.

63.why: Today's air is oxidizing (oxygen-rich) and has almost no hydrogen.

64.why: Cellulose's β-1,4 links form rigid, cross-linked fibers. Starch's α links don't.

65.why: Glucose + fructose → sucrose + water: a dehydration reaction.

66.why: Trans fats are unsaturated fats with the hydrogens on opposite sides of the double bond.

69.why: Arginine is positively charged, now sitting in a nonpolar stretch, which could change bonding there.

70.why: It may do nothing, or a lot, like the single swap that causes sickle cell.

71.why: HIV's RNA copying is error-prone, so it mutates fast.

72.why: Hershey and Chase labeled DNA and protein differently. Only the DNA entered the host.

73.why: Only the third codon changed (GTA → GAA): a single-base substitution.

74.why: DNA changes are copied to daughter cells, so they're permanent.
